claims.subject: rsp-v2-0
claims.statement: Did RSP v2.0’s changes to threshold and mitigation specification reduce the verifiability of Anthropic’s safety commitments relative to v1.0?

time.note: v2.0’s effective date; the assessments were published afterwards (SaferAI on 2024-10-23).

claims.qualification: Unresolved open question, not a finding. SaferAI characterises the revision as replacing precise thresholds and mitigation specifications with qualitative descriptions; Anthropic describes greater flexibility and retained core safeguards. These passages do not establish opposing assessments of verifiability. SaferAI judges that the change reduces transparency and accountability and asks stakeholders to trust Anthropic rather than providing verifiable commitments and metrics, and it lowered Anthropic’s rating from 2.2 to 1.9; the record holds this criticism but no direct opposing assessment of verifiability, so every passage is context. The textual changes are recorded separately, and the record does not decide the question.

claims.subject: rsp-v3-0
claims.statement: Whether RSP v3.0’s new roadmap and transparency mechanisms compensate for its reduced unilateral commitments, in the policy’s overall capacity to secure risk mitigation, remains unsettled.

time.note: v3.0’s effective date; the assessments were published on and after that date.

claims.qualification: Unresolved open question, not a finding; it keeps the strength of the commitments apart from their expected effectiveness. Both sides accept the main changes: v3.0 drops the implied unilateral commitment to pause development and deployment when required safeguards cannot be met, separates recommendations for the industry from what Anthropic commits to as a company, adds transparency commitments, and introduces roadmap goals that are public goals rather than hard commitments. TIME’s report judges that overall the change leaves Anthropic far less constrained by its own safety policies. Sophie Williams and Jonas Freund, writing on GovAI’s site in a post that represents their own views, judge that it weakened future security commitments, note that existing mitigations are not lowered and conclude on balance that honesty about constraints is better than commitments that would not be followed; their article was updated on 2026-03-17 on competitor-matching commitments, and the quoted passages are unchanged. Anthropic describes the revision as amplifying what worked and committing it to more transparency. Holden Karnofsky, who led the revision and writes in his own name, expects more specific and realistic goals to improve their forcing function despite weaker consequences for missing them, and leaves the net effect uncertain. Jared Kaplan, Anthropic’s chief science officer, told TIME that unilateral commitments made no sense while competitors pressed ahead, and denied that the change was a U-turn or a capitulation to market incentives. METR’s Chris Painter, who reviewed an early draft with Anthropic’s permission, called the change understandable but was concerned it might enable a gradual “frog-boiling” effect. None of these passages settles whether the new mechanisms compensate, so all are context. The textual changes are recorded separately, and the record does not decide the question.

claims.subject: preparedness-v2

object.value: Whether Version 2’s governance arrangements permit OpenAI Leadership to deploy High-capability models without sufficient safeguards

claims.statement: Preparedness Framework v2’s governance arrangements permit OpenAI Leadership to deploy models with High capabilities without safeguards that sufficiently minimize their associated risks.

time.note: Dated by the edition. OpenAI’s announcement was published with it on 2025-04-15 and the ChatGPT agent system card on 2025-07-17; Coggins et al. submitted v1 of their analysis on 2025-09-29 and revised it as v2 on 2025-10-13.

claims.qualification: Contested assessment of the policy’s permissiveness, not a finding that OpenAI deployed a model without safeguards, a legal ruling or a guarantee of compliance. Coggins et al. (arXiv:2509.24394; v1 2025-09-29, v2 2025-10-13) read the framework’s governance arrangements as letting OpenAI Leadership, the CEO or a person designated by them, approve or reject the Safety Advisory Group’s recommendations and so deploy even more dangerous capabilities, especially if other developers do so. OpenAI’s announcement of Version 2 states that covered systems reaching High capability must have safeguards that sufficiently minimize the associated risk of severe harm before they are deployed, and its ChatGPT agent system card describes the framework as committing it to such safeguards; both predate the analysis and are not replies to it. The record does not decide whether leadership’s authority over the recommendations defeats that stated requirement. The paper’s framework-wide conclusion and OpenAI’s comparison of Version 2 with its predecessor are context. The rule’s own wording is recorded in prov-preparedness-v2-high-deployment-restriction.

claims.subject: openai-group-pbc

object.value: Whether the OpenAI Foundation can exercise effective mission-directed control over OpenAI Group PBC in practice after the October 2025 recapitalization

claims.statement: Following the October 2025 recapitalization, the OpenAI Foundation can exercise effective mission-directed control over OpenAI Group PBC in practice.

time.note: The cited passages were published between 28 October 2025 (OpenAI’s announcement and the Delaware Attorney General’s letter) and 11 May 2026 (Fried and Reiter). OpenAI’s structure page is undated.

claims.qualification: Effective control here concerns the Foundation’s ability to enforce its mission through its retained governance powers when commercial interests or Group management resist. OpenAI asserts continuing control; formal rights are documented separately. Bret Taylor’s announcement for OpenAI’s board says the recapitalization keeps the mission at the center and maintains the strongest representation of mission-focused governance in the industry. Not For Private Gain recognises improvements over the abandoned proposal while judging control weaker than under the former structure and identifying conditional risks to effective exercise. CalMatters reports critics’ concerns about possible commercial predominance. Fried and Reiter describe the Foundation’s appointment, veto and safety-blocking powers as substantial authority over investors and argue that guardians may do too much as well as too little. The Delaware Attorney General’s non-objection is conditional on representations. These sources do not settle practical effectiveness, and no legal conclusion or side is adopted.

claims.subject: anthropic

object.value: Whether Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust is independent enough of stockholders to exercise effective public-interest oversight of Anthropic in practice

claims.statement: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust has sufficient independence from stockholders to exercise effective public-interest oversight of Anthropic in practice.

time.note: The cited passages were published between 19 September 2023 and 9 July 2026; the Transparency Hub passage is from the version last updated 23 July 2026.

claims.qualification: The unresolved question is whether the Trust can exercise effective public-interest oversight when stockholder preferences conflict with that oversight. Anthropic describes financially disinterested Trustees, an intended independent design and a checking role; its Transparency Hub says the Trust’s authority to elect directors helps insulate the mission from short-term commercial and shareholder pressures, and its April 2026 announcement says Trust-appointed directors then formed a board majority. Appointment power is distinct from independence against removal. Stein-Perlman’s 2024 analysis tentatively identifies possible stockholder subordination under incompletely disclosed failsafe terms. Fried and Reiter describe partial investor insulation and favour constraints on guardian overreach; they do not simply deny an effective checking role. Outside counsel describe the arrangement’s accountability and amendment mechanisms. Source dates and subsequent phase-in must be distinguished. The inspected public descriptions do not settle practical effectiveness; no side or legal conclusion is adopted.
